    Independent: "I am confident, creative". Interdependent: "I am a good son, a loyal friend". The self is defined by relationships.

    Ways of knowing oneself

    1 · Introspection

    Looking inward at our own thoughts and feelings. Limited: we often don't know why we do things, and we may invent reasons (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977).

    2 · Self-perception theory (Bem, 1972)

    When our inner feelings are unclear, we infer them by observing our own behaviour, like an outsider. "I go to the gym daily, so I must like fitness."

    3 · Social comparison (Festinger, 1954)

    We judge our abilities and opinions by comparing with others. Upward comparison (with better) can inspire or depress; downward (with worse) boosts self-esteem.

    4 · Feedback from others

    Others' reactions (the looking-glass self) and what close people tell us.

    Overjustification effect

    Self-perception also explains why rewarding an enjoyable activity can reduce intrinsic interest: "I'm doing it for the reward, not because I like it" (Lepper, Greene & Nisbett, 1973).

    RememberI-S-S-F: Introspection, Self-perception, Social comparison, Feedback.

    Self-control

    Self-control (self-regulation) is the ability to override impulses and act toward long-term goals.

    Ego depletion (Baumeister)

    Self-control may work like a muscle that gets tired with use: after resisting cookies, people gave up sooner on puzzles. Later large studies found this effect much weaker than first reported, so mention it with caution.

    Strategies that help
    • Avoid temptation (remove the phone)
    • Implementation intentions: "If X, then I will do Y"
    • Distraction and "cool" thinking (Mischel)
    • Rest, sleep, glucose, positive mood

    Self-esteem

    Self-esteem is our overall evaluation of ourselves: the attitude we hold toward ourselves, positive or negative.

    Measurement

    Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (10 items) for explicit self-esteem; the Implicit Association Test for implicit self-esteem.

    Sources

    Feedback from others, social comparison, success in areas that matter to us.

    Sociometer theory

    Self-esteem is a gauge of how accepted and included we are (Leary).

    High self-esteem

    • Happier, more persistent after failure
    • Less depression
    • But very high, unstable self-esteem can become narcissism and aggression when threatened

    Low self-esteem

    • Linked with depression, anxiety
    • More sensitive to rejection
    • Self-handicapping (making excuses in advance)

    Self-esteem tends to drop in adolescence (especially for girls), rise through adulthood, and fall again in old age.

    LF
    Leon Festinger (1919–1989)American social psychologist. A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957). Also proposed social comparison theory (1954).

    Cognitive dissonance

    Cognitive dissonance is the unpleasant tension we feel when we hold two inconsistent cognitions, or when our behaviour contradicts our attitudes.

    Because it feels bad, we are motivated to reduce it, often by changing our attitude to fit what we did.

    RememberReduce dissonance with B-A-C-T: change Behaviour, change Attitude, add Consonant thoughts, Trivialise.

    The $1 / $20 experiment (Festinger & Carlsmith, 1959)

    Students did a very boring task (turning pegs) for an hour. They were then paid $1 or $20 to tell the next person it was fun. Later they rated how enjoyable the task really was (scale −5 to +5).

    Other forms of dissonance

    Induced compliance

    Being led to act against our attitude with little reward (the $1 study). Less reward → more attitude change.

    Effort justification

    We value what we suffered for. Aronson & Mills (1959): a severe initiation made a dull group discussion seem more interesting.

    Post-decision dissonance

    After choosing, we rate the chosen option higher and the rejected one lower ("spreading of alternatives", Brehm, 1956).

    Hypocrisy induction

    Reminding people that they preach something they don't practise makes them change behaviour (e.g. condom use, water saving).

    Alternative view: Bem's self-perception theory explains the $1 result without any tension: people simply infer their attitude from their behaviour.

    Aggression

    Aggression is behaviour intended to harm another person who wants to avoid that harm. Accidental harm is not aggression; an intended but failed attack is.

    Hostile (reactive) aggression

    Driven by anger; harm is the goal. "He insulted me, so I hit him."

    Instrumental aggression

    Harm is a means to another goal: robbery, a contract killing.

    Direct vs indirect

    Direct: physical or verbal attack. Indirect (relational): gossip, exclusion, spreading rumours.

    Views on aggression

    1 · Instinct theories

    Freud: Thanatos, the death instinct, turned outward. Konrad Lorenz: a fighting instinct that evolved for survival.

    2 · Biological and evolutionary

    Testosterone, low serotonin, brain areas (amygdala, prefrontal cortex), genetics. Evolution: male aggression over status and mates.

    3 · Drive theories: frustration–aggression hypothesis

    Dollard et al. (1939): frustration always leads to aggression, and aggression always comes from frustration. Berkowitz revised it: frustration causes anger, which leads to aggression especially when aggressive cues are present (the weapons effect, 1967).

    4 · Social learning theory (Bandura)

    Aggression is learned by observing and imitating models, especially rewarded ones.

    Albert Bandura (1961) · Bobo doll studyChildren who watched an adult hit and kick an inflatable Bobo doll copied the same aggressive acts, even the exact words used.Photo: CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

    General Aggression Model (Anderson & Bushman, 2002)

    Factors that increase aggression

    • Provocation and frustration; hostile attribution bias (seeing others' acts as deliberately hostile)
    • Violent media and video games
    • Heat (more violence on hot days), alcohol, crowding, noise
    • Culture of honour, gender norms, deindividuation in crowds

    Reducing aggression

    • Punishment that is prompt, certain and strong, but it can model aggression too
    • Catharsis is mostly a myth: "venting" (hitting a pillow) usually increases later aggression (Bushman, 2002)
    • Cognitive strategies: apologies, pre-attribution (explaining the situation), delaying responses
    • Teaching social skills, empathy, and non-aggressive models

    Unit III self-test

    Who proposed the looking-glass self?

    Charles Horton Cooley (1902).

    What is self-perception theory?

    Bem (1972): when feelings are unclear, we infer them from our own behaviour.

    Upward vs downward comparison?

    Upward = with people better off (can inspire or deflate); downward = with people worse off (boosts self-esteem).

    Define cognitive dissonance.

    Unpleasant tension from inconsistent cognitions, especially when behaviour contradicts attitudes.

    Which group in Festinger & Carlsmith rated the task most enjoyable?

    The $1 group (insufficient justification).

    What is effort justification?

    Valuing something more because we suffered to get it (Aronson & Mills, 1959).

    Hostile vs instrumental aggression?

    Hostile: harm is the goal, driven by anger. Instrumental: harm is a means to another goal.

    Does catharsis reduce aggression?

    Mostly no: venting usually increases later aggression.

    Long-answer outlines

    Discuss the nature and origins of the self-concept and ways of knowing oneself. 10 marks
    1. Definition; James's I and me; self-schema.
    2. Origins: Cooley, Mead, mirror test, roles, culture (draw independent vs interdependent).
    3. Ways of knowing: introspection, self-perception, social comparison, feedback.
    4. Self-control and self-esteem briefly.
    Explain Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; examples.
    2. Ways to reduce dissonance (draw).
    3. $1/$20 study (chart).
    4. Induced compliance, effort justification, post-decision dissonance, hypocrisy.
    5. Criticism: self-perception theory; conclusion.
    Describe social psychological views on aggression. 10 marks
    1. Definition and types.
    2. Instinct, biological, frustration–aggression (Berkowitz revision), social learning (Bobo doll).
    3. General Aggression Model (draw).
    4. Factors and ways of reducing aggression.
    Advanced Social Psychology · Unit IV

    Attitudes and Prejudice

    What is an attitude?

    An attitude is an evaluation of any aspect of the social world (a person, object, idea, issue) as positive or negative, favourable or unfavourable.

    G. W. Allport (1935)

    "A mental and neural state of readiness, organised through experience, exerting a directive or dynamic influence upon the individual's response to all objects and situations with which it is related."

    Features
    • Learned, not inborn
    • Have direction (+/−) and strength
    • Fairly stable, but can change
    • Guide behaviour

    ABC model: three components

    RememberAttitudes are as easy as ABC: Affect, Behaviour, Cognition.

    How attitudes form

    Classical conditioning

    Pairing an object with pleasant or unpleasant feelings (adverts with happy music). Can be subliminal.

    Instrumental conditioning

    Being rewarded or punished for expressing an attitude.

    Observational learning

    Copying the attitudes of parents, peers and media figures.

    Social comparison

    Adopting the views of groups we identify with.

    Do attitudes predict behaviour?

    Key study · LaPiere, 1934

    Attitudes ≠ behaviour

    LaPiere travelled across the USA with a Chinese couple. They were refused service only once in 251 places. Yet when he later wrote asking whether these places would serve Chinese guests, over 90% of those that replied said no.

    Attitudes predict behaviour better when they are strong (extreme, certain, from personal experience), specific to the behaviour, and accessible.

    Theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen, 1991)

    Attitude toward the behaviour + subjective norms (what others expect) + perceived behavioural control → intention → behaviour.

    Explicit and implicit attitudes

    Explicit attitudes

    Conscious, deliberate, easy to report. Measured by questionnaires and rating scales (Likert, semantic differential).

    "I believe men and women are equally good at science."

    Implicit attitudes

    Automatic, often unconscious, hard to control. Can differ from explicit attitudes.

    Faster to link "male" with "science" despite saying otherwise.

    Measurement · Greenwald et al., 1998

    Implicit Association Test (IAT)

    Measures how quickly people sort words or faces into paired categories (e.g. "young + good" vs "old + good"). Faster pairing suggests a stronger automatic association.

    Why it matters: explicit attitudes predict deliberate behaviour (voting); implicit attitudes predict spontaneous behaviour (body language, seating distance). The IAT's reliability for predicting an individual's behaviour is debated.

    Attitude change: persuasion

    Yale approach (Hovland, 1950s): who says what to whom

    Communicator (who)

    Credible (expert, trustworthy), attractive and similar sources persuade more. Fast speakers often seem more credible.

    Message (what)

    Messages that don't seem designed to persuade work better. Fear appeals work if they also show how to avoid the danger. Two-sided messages for informed audiences.

    Audience (to whom)

    Mood, intelligence, self-esteem and age affect persuasion. People in a good mood are easier to persuade.

    Sleeper effect: a message from a low-credibility source can become more persuasive over time, as people forget the source.

    Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)

    A similar model is Chaiken's heuristic–systematic model.

    Other routes to attitude change, and resisting persuasion

    Cognitive dissonance

    Acting against our attitude (with little justification) changes the attitude (see Unit III).

    Resisting persuasion
    • Reactance: pushing back when we feel our freedom is threatened
    • Forewarning: knowing persuasion is coming
    • Selective avoidance of opposing information
    • Inoculation (McGuire): exposure to weak counter-arguments builds resistance, like a vaccine
    • Biased assimilation: evidence against our view seems weaker

    Prejudice

    Prejudice is a negative attitude toward members of a social group, based only on their membership in that group.

    Stereotype · Cognitive

    Beliefs about a group's traits: "group X are lazy".

    Prejudice · Affective

    Negative feelings toward the group.

    Discrimination · Behavioural

    Unfair negative actions toward group members.

    Prejudice follows the ABC structure of attitudes. Examples: caste, religion, gender, region, skin colour, disability, sexual orientation.

    Development: how prejudice is learned

    • Socialisation: children pick up attitudes from parents (by about age 5 they can show racial preferences).
    • Social learning: rewarded for expressing the "right" views; imitating peers.
    • Media: repeated stereotyped portrayals.
    • Social norms: what one's community treats as normal.

    Causes of prejudice

    1 · Realistic conflict theory

    Competition for scarce resources (jobs, land) creates hostility.

    2 · Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979)

    We boost self-esteem by seeing our group as better than others (in-group favouritism).

    3 · Social categorisation

    Dividing the world into "us" and "them". Out-group homogeneity: "they are all the same".

    4 · Cognitive sources

    Stereotypes save mental effort; illusory correlation links minority groups with rare (negative) behaviour.

    5 · Personality

    Authoritarian personality (Adorno et al., 1950): rigid, obedient to authority, hostile to out-groups. Also social dominance orientation.

    6 · Frustration and scapegoating

    Displacing anger onto a weaker group (e.g. blaming migrants for economic problems).

    Key study · Sherif, 1954

    Robbers Cave experiment

    Boys at a summer camp were split into two groups, "Eagles" and "Rattlers". Competition for prizes quickly produced name-calling and raids. Friendly contact alone didn't fix it; superordinate goals (tasks needing both groups, like fixing the water supply) reduced hostility.

    Henri Tajfel · minimal group paradigm (1970s)Even groups formed on trivial grounds (preferring Klee or Kandinsky paintings) favoured their own members when sharing rewards.Photo: European Association of Social Psychology, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Effects of prejudice

    Stereotype threat

    Fear of confirming a negative stereotype lowers performance. Black students did worse on a test described as measuring intelligence (Steele & Aronson, 1995).

    Self-fulfilling prophecy

    Low expectations lead to poor treatment, which leads to poor outcomes.

    Health and well-being

    Chronic stress, anxiety, depression, poorer physical health.

    Social

    Discrimination in jobs, housing, education; conflict and violence.

    Reducing prejudice

    Gordon Allport · The Nature of Prejudice (1954)Proposed the contact hypothesis.Photo: C. George Boeree, Free Art License, Wikimedia Commons

    Contact hypothesis: contact works under four conditions

    1 · Equal status

    Groups meet as equals.

    2 · Common goals

    Working toward shared goals.

    3 · Cooperation

    Interdependence, not competition.

    4 · Support of authorities

    Laws, norms, leaders back the contact.

    RememberE-C-C-S: "Equal Classmates Cooperate Successfully."

    Other strategies

    Recategorisation

    Common in-group identity model: turn "us and them" into "we" (e.g. "we are all Indians").

    Jigsaw classroom (Aronson)

    Each student holds one piece of the lesson, so everyone depends on each other.

    Learning not to hate

    Parents and teachers modelling tolerance; education.

    Extended contact

    Knowing that an in-group friend has an out-group friend reduces prejudice.

    Cognitive interventions

    Training to "just say no" to stereotypes; perspective-taking; awareness of implicit bias.

    Social influence

    Showing that peers hold tolerant attitudes changes norms.

    Unit IV self-test

    Three components of an attitude?

    Affective, behavioural, cognitive (ABC).

    What did LaPiere (1934) show?

    Stated attitudes did not match actual behaviour: he and a Chinese couple were refused service only once, yet most establishments said in writing they would refuse.

    What does the IAT measure?

    Implicit attitudes, through reaction times to paired categories.

    Central vs peripheral route?

    Central: careful thought about arguments, lasting change. Peripheral: superficial cues, short-lived change.

    Stereotype, prejudice, discrimination?

    Belief (cognitive), feeling (affective), action (behavioural).

    What reduced hostility in Robbers Cave?

    Superordinate goals that required cooperation.

    Allport's four conditions for contact?

    Equal status, common goals, cooperation, support of authorities.

    What is stereotype threat?

    Fear of confirming a negative stereotype, which lowers performance.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the nature and components of attitudes, and explicit vs implicit attitudes. 10 marks
    1. Definition; features.
    2. ABC model (draw).
    3. Formation.
    4. Explicit vs implicit; IAT.
    5. Attitude–behaviour link: LaPiere, planned behaviour.
    Discuss attitude change. 10 marks
    1. Yale approach: communicator, message, audience.
    2. ELM (draw).
    3. Dissonance.
    4. Resistance to persuasion.
    Explain the causes of prejudice and ways to reduce it. 10 marks
    1. Definition; stereotype–prejudice–discrimination.
    2. Development.
    3. Causes: realistic conflict (Robbers Cave), social identity, categorisation, cognitive, personality, scapegoating.
    4. Effects.
    5. Reduction: contact hypothesis, recategorisation, jigsaw, others.
    Advanced Social Psychology · Unit V

    Social Influence and Group Processes

    Social influence and conformity

    Social influence is the effort by one or more people to change the attitudes, beliefs or behaviour of others. Conformity means changing our behaviour to match social norms, the rules about how we ought to behave.

    Conformity

    Going along with the group, without being directly asked.

    Compliance

    Agreeing to a direct request.

    Obedience

    Following a command from an authority figure.

    Descriptive norms

    What most people do: "most people here don't litter".

    Injunctive norms

    What people ought to do: "littering is wrong".

    Classic studies

    Key study · Sherif, 1935

    Autokinetic effect

    In a dark room, a still point of light seems to move. Alone, people gave very different estimates of the movement. In groups, their estimates converged on a shared norm, which they kept even when tested alone later. This is informational influence in an ambiguous situation.

    SA
    Solomon Asch (1951, 1956)Line-judgement studies: conformity even when the right answer is obvious.
    Key study · Asch, 1951–56

    Line judgement

    A real participant sat with 6–8 confederates who, on 12 of 18 trials, all gave the same obviously wrong answer about which line matched a standard line. Alone, people made almost no errors (under 1%).

    • Participants conformed on about 37% of critical trials
    • About 75% conformed at least once
    • About 25% never conformed

    Why do we conform? (Deutsch & Gerard, 1955)

    Normative influence

    The desire to be liked and accepted, and fear of rejection. Leads to public compliance without private agreement (Asch).

    Informational influence

    The desire to be right: we treat others as a source of information, especially when uncertain. Leads to real private acceptance (Sherif).

    Factors affecting conformity

    Cohesiveness

    We conform more to groups we like and belong to.

    Group size

    Rises up to about 3–4 people, then levels off.

    Unanimity

    One ally breaks the pressure.

    Public response

    More conformity when answers are public.

    Culture

    Higher in collectivist cultures.

    Task difficulty

    Harder or ambiguous tasks → more informational conformity.

    Conformity bias

    Conformity bias is our tendency to behave like the people around us rather than use our own independent judgement, and to underestimate how much we are influenced. Most people believe "others conform, but I don't".

    Pluralistic ignorance

    Everyone privately disagrees with a norm but wrongly thinks others accept it, so the norm continues (e.g. heavy drinking at college parties).

    Introspection illusion

    We judge ourselves by our inner thoughts ("I chose freely") and others by their behaviour ("they just copied").

    Impact of feedback

    Feedback from the group strongly shapes conformity:

    • Social approval (smiles, praise, inclusion) for agreeing increases conformity. Social disapproval and rejection for disagreeing push people back into line. Even seeing someone else rejected increases conformity.
    • Feedback about accuracy: if people learn the group was often wrong, they conform less; if the group is shown to be right, informational conformity grows.
    • Normative feedback ("your neighbours use less electricity than you") changes behaviour toward the norm; this is used in energy-saving campaigns.
    • Feedback that confirms our own competence (e.g. being told we are an expert) reduces conformity.

    Non-conformity: resisting group pressure

    Need for individuation

    The wish to be distinct and unique from others.

    Need for control

    People with a high desire for control resist pressure more.

    Reactance

    Pushing back when we feel our freedom is threatened.

    Social support

    Having even one ally who disagrees with the group.

    Idiosyncrasy credits

    People who have conformed in the past "earn credits" that let them deviate later without rejection.

    Power

    High-power people conform less.

    Minority influence · Moscovici, 1969

    The consistent minority

    A minority that consistently called blue slides "green" influenced the majority's later colour judgements. A consistent, confident minority can change majority views, often slowly and privately.

    Stanley Milgram (1933–1984)Yale University. Obedience to Authority (1974). He was inspired by the trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Obedience to authority

    Obedience is following the direct orders of an authority figure. Can ordinary people be made to harm others simply because they are told to?

    Key study · Milgram, 1963

    The "shock" experiment

    Participants, as "teachers", were told to give electric shocks to a "learner" (a confederate) for each wrong answer, rising in 15-volt steps from 15 V to 450 V. No real shocks were given, but the learner screamed, protested, then fell silent. When teachers hesitated, the experimenter used prods such as "The experiment requires that you continue."

    Psychiatrists predicted almost no one would go to the end. In fact 65% obeyed all the way to 450 V.

    Why do people obey?

    Agentic state

    People see themselves as an "agent" carrying out another's wishes, so they shift responsibility to the authority.

    Legitimate authority

    Uniforms, titles, a prestigious setting (Yale) increase obedience.

    Gradual escalation (foot-in-the-door)

    Small 15-volt steps made each next step feel only slightly worse.

    Norms of obedience

    We are taught from childhood to obey parents, teachers, police.

    Resisting destructive obedience

    • Remind people that they are responsible for harm
    • Teach that blind obedience is inappropriate; question authority's motives
    • Disobedient models: seeing others refuse
    • Know about the research: awareness itself helps

    Ethics and replication: Milgram's study caused severe stress and used deception, and led to stricter ethics rules. Burger (2009) ran a safer partial replication (stopping at 150 V) and found obedience rates similar to Milgram's.

    What is a group?

    A group is two or more people who interact, are interdependent, share common goals, and see themselves as a unit. A crowd at a bus stop is not a group; a cricket team is.

    Entitativity

    How much a collection of people is seen as a real, unified group. High for families and teams; low for people in a queue.

    Roles

    Expected behaviours for each position (captain, secretary).

    Status

    Rank or prestige within the group.

    Norms

    Rules about how members should behave.

    Cohesiveness

    Forces that bind members together; liking and commitment.

    Why do people join groups? (functions)

    Belonging

    Basic need for affiliation, love and acceptance.

    Self-knowledge

    Groups help us know who we are (social comparison).

    Identity and self-esteem

    Group membership adds to self-concept and pride.

    Achieving goals

    Doing together what we can't do alone.

    Security and protection

    Safety in numbers, support in hard times.

    Information

    Learning from others, reducing uncertainty.

    RememberWe join groups for B-S-I-G-S-I: "Belonging, Self-knowledge, Identity, Goals, Security, Information."

    Stages of group development (Tuckman, 1965)

    Forming1

    Getting to know each other; uncertainty.

    Storming2

    Conflict over roles and leadership.

    Norming3

    Agreement on norms and roles; cohesion grows.

    Performing4

    Working effectively toward goals.

    Adjourning5

    Group ends after the task (added in 1977).

    Social loafing

    Social loafing is the tendency to put in less effort when working in a group on a shared task, where individual contributions are pooled and not identifiable, than when working alone.

    Key study · Ringelmann, 1880s (published 1913)

    Rope pulling

    As more men pulled a rope together, the force per person fell.

    Key study · Latané, Williams & Harkins, 1979

    Clapping and shouting

    Blindfolded students wearing headphones shouted or clapped "alone" or "with others". They made less noise per person when they believed others were also shouting, even when they were actually alone. So the drop is due to reduced effort, not just poor coordination.

    Why it happens: collective effort model (Karau & Williams, 1993)

    People work hard only when they believe their effort will matter for an outcome they value. In groups, each person's effort feels less important and less noticed.

    Reducing social loafing

    Identifiability

    Make each person's contribution visible.

    Commitment

    Increase commitment to the task's success.

    Importance

    Make the task meaningful and valued.

    Unique contribution

    Give each member a distinct, necessary role.

    Small groups and cohesion

    Friends and small teams loaf less.

    Loafing is weaker in collectivist cultures and among women. The opposite, social compensation, happens when people work harder to make up for weak teammates on an important task.

    Group decision-making

    How groups reach decisions: social decision schemes

    Majority-wins

    The view held by most members is chosen. The most common rule.

    Truth-wins

    The correct answer wins once its correctness is recognised.

    First-shift

    The group adopts the direction of the first person who changes position.

    Group polarisation

    Group discussion makes members' views more extreme in the direction they already leaned. First found as the "risky shift" (Stoner, 1961), then shown to work in either direction (Moscovici & Zavalloni, 1969).

    Why? (1) Social comparison: members want to seem "better" than average in the valued direction. (2) Persuasive arguments: discussion brings out more arguments on the favoured side.

    Groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972)

    IJ
    Irving JanisStudied disastrous US decisions such as the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion.

    Groupthink happens when a highly cohesive group cares more about agreement than about making the right decision.

    Causes
    • High cohesiveness
    • Isolation from outside views
    • A strong, directive leader
    • High stress, time pressure
    Symptoms
    • Illusion of invulnerability
    • Belief in the group's morality
    • Collective rationalisation
    • Stereotyping opponents
    • Pressure on dissenters
    • Self-censorship
    • Illusion of unanimity
    • Self-appointed "mindguards"

    Preventing groupthink

    • The leader stays impartial and invites criticism
    • Assign a devil's advocate; encourage authentic dissent
    • Use sub-groups and outside experts
    • Hold a "second-chance" meeting before finalising

    Other problems in group decisions

    Biased information sampling

    Groups discuss information everyone already shares and ignore unique information held by individuals (the "hidden profile", Stasser & Titus, 1985).

    Escalation of commitment

    Continuing to invest in a failing decision because of what has already been spent (sunk cost).

    Unit V self-test

    Normative vs informational influence?

    Normative: wanting to be liked. Informational: wanting to be right.

    Asch's main results?

    Conformity on about 37% of critical trials; about 75% conformed at least once.

    Effect of one dissenting ally in Asch's study?

    Conformity dropped sharply, to about 5%.

    What is pluralistic ignorance?

    Everyone privately disagrees with a norm but thinks others accept it.

    Percent who obeyed to 450 V in Milgram's baseline?

    65%.

    What is the agentic state?

    Seeing oneself as an agent carrying out another's orders, shifting responsibility to the authority.

    Define social loafing.

    Reduced effort when working in a group on a pooled task compared with working alone.

    Who proposed groupthink?

    Irving Janis (1972).

    What is group polarisation?

    Group discussion makes members' initial leanings more extreme.

    Tuckman's stages?

    Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.

    Long-answer outlines

    Discuss social conformity with classic studies. 10 marks
    1. Social influence; conformity vs compliance vs obedience; norms.
    2. Sherif and Asch (with chart).
    3. Normative vs informational influence; factors.
    4. Conformity bias, feedback, non-conformity, minority influence.
    Explain obedience to authority. 10 marks
    1. Definition; Eichmann background.
    2. Milgram's procedure and results; variations (chart).
    3. Reasons for obedience.
    4. Resisting obedience; ethics; Burger's replication.
    Describe groups, social loafing and group decision-making. 10 marks
    1. Meaning of group; components; why people join; Tuckman.
    2. Social loafing: Ringelmann (chart), Latané; reducing it.
    3. Decision schemes; polarisation; groupthink (causes, symptoms, prevention).
    Foundations of Psychology · Unit I

    Introduction to Psychology

    What is psychology?

    The word comes from Greek: psyche (soul or mind) + logos (study). So it began as the "study of the soul". Over time the definition changed as psychology became a science.

    Study of soulAncient Greece

    Philosophers (Plato, Aristotle) discussed the soul. It could not be observed, so this was dropped.

    Study of mind17th–18th c.

    Philosophers studied the mind and its faculties. "Mind" was vague.

    Study of consciousness1879 onward

    Wundt and William James studied conscious experience, mainly through introspection.

    Study of behaviour1913 onward

    J. B. Watson: psychology should study only observable behaviour.

    Behaviour + mental processesToday

    Modern definition: the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.

    RememberPsychology "lost its soul, then its mind, then its consciousness, and found behaviour" (a remark often attributed to R. S. Woodworth).

    Definitions to quote

    Modern definition (e.g. Baron; Feldman)

    "Psychology is the science of behaviour and mental processes."

    J. B. Watson (1913)

    Psychology is "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science" whose goal is the prediction and control of behaviour.

    Behaviour

    Anything an organism does that can be observed: walking, talking, blushing, smiling.

    Mental processes

    Inner experiences we infer from behaviour: thinking, memory, emotion, perception, dreams.

    Nature of psychology

    A science

    Uses the scientific method, observation and experiment.

    Studies the individual

    Mostly individual behaviour, in social and biological context.

    Biological and social

    A bio-psycho-social science: brain, mind and society all matter.

    Pure and applied

    Basic research builds knowledge; applied research solves real problems.

    Positive (descriptive)

    Describes how people do behave, not how they should.

    Many approaches

    Biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, humanistic, cognitive, sociocultural.

    Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920)Set up the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig, Germany, in 1879, the "birth year" of scientific psychology. Called the father of experimental psychology.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Is psychology a science?

    Yes. A subject is a science because of its method, not its topic. Psychology uses the scientific method.

    Characteristics that make psychology scientific

    Empirical

    Based on observation and evidence, not opinion.

    Objective

    Results don't depend on the researcher's personal feelings.

    Systematic

    Follows planned, orderly procedures.

    Verifiable and replicable

    Other researchers can repeat the study and check results.

    Controlled

    Experiments control other variables to find cause and effect.

    Predictive

    Builds theories that predict behaviour.

    RememberE-O-S-V-C-P: "Every Observation Should Verify Cause and Prediction."

    Limits: human behaviour is complex and changes with context; the observer can affect what is observed; some topics (consciousness) are hard to measure; ethics limit experiments. So psychology is sometimes called a "young" or "soft" science.

    Four goals of psychology

    1 · Description

    Observing and recording behaviour accurately.

    "Riya gets anxious before exams."

    2 · Explanation

    Finding the causes; building theories.

    "Because she believes failing would disappoint her parents."

    3 · Prediction

    Forecasting when behaviour will happen.

    "She will be anxious before the next unit test."

    4 · Control (application)

    Changing or improving behaviour to improve lives.

    "Relaxation training and cognitive reframing reduce her anxiety."

    RememberD-E-P-C: "Doctors Examine, Predict, Cure."

    Branches of psychology

    BranchStudiesExample question
    General / ExperimentalBasic processes: learning, memory, perceptionHow do we forget?
    BiopsychologyBrain, nervous system, hormonesWhich brain area controls fear?
    DevelopmentalChange across the life spanWhen do children learn to talk?
    SocialInfluence of othersWhy do people conform?
    CognitiveThinking, problem solving, languageHow do we make decisions?
    ClinicalDiagnosis and treatment of mental disordersHow to treat depression?
    CounsellingEveryday adjustment problemsHow to cope with exam stress?
    Educational / SchoolTeaching and learning; children in schoolHow to help a slow learner?
    Industrial-OrganisationalPeople at workHow to motivate employees?
    HealthPsychology of illness and healthWhy do people keep smoking?
    ForensicPsychology and lawIs this eyewitness reliable?
    Sports, Environmental, Positive, CommunityNewer applied fieldsHow does nature reduce stress?

    Scope: where psychology is used

    Health

    Hospitals, mental health clinics, rehabilitation centres

    Education

    Schools, guidance, special education

    Work

    HR, selection, training, ergonomics

    Law and defence

    Courts, police, armed forces selection (e.g. SSB)

    Society

    Reducing prejudice, public campaigns, disaster relief

    Research and teaching

    Universities, research institutes

    Schools of psychology (brief)

    StructuralismWundt, Titchener

    Break consciousness into elements through introspection.

    FunctionalismWilliam James

    What is the purpose (function) of the mind?

    PsychoanalysisFreud

    The unconscious and childhood.

    BehaviourismWatson, Skinner

    Only observable behaviour; learning.

    GestaltWertheimer, Köhler

    "The whole is different from the sum of its parts."

    HumanisticMaslow, Rogers

    Free will, growth, self-actualisation.

    Cognitive1950s–60s

    Mind as information processor.

    Unit I self-test

    Greek roots of "psychology"?

    Psyche (soul/mind) + logos (study).

    Modern definition of psychology?

    The scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.

    Who founded the first psychology lab, and when?

    Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig, 1879.

    Four goals of psychology?

    Describe, explain, predict, control.

    Clinical vs counselling psychology?

    Clinical deals with mental disorders; counselling with everyday adjustment problems.

    Who founded behaviourism?

    John B. Watson (1913).

    Long-answer outlines

    Discuss the concept and nature of psychology. Is psychology a science? 10 marks
    1. Origin of the word; changing definitions (timeline).
    2. Modern definition; behaviour and mental processes.
    3. Nature of psychology.
    4. Scientific method (draw cycle) and scientific characteristics.
    5. Limits; conclusion.
    Explain the goals, branches and scope of psychology. 10 marks
    1. Four goals with one example each (draw steps).
    2. Main branches (table).
    3. Scope in fields of life.
    Foundations of Psychology · Unit II

    Learning

    What is learning?

    Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour (or behaviour potential) that results from experience or practice.

    Relatively permanent

    Temporary changes (fatigue, drugs, illness) are not learning.

    Change in behaviour

    Can be good or bad: learning to smoke is also learning.

    Through experience

    Changes due to maturation (growing up, e.g. walking) are not learning.

    Nature of learning

    • It is a process, inferred from performance (we can't see learning directly).
    • It is universal and continuous, from birth to death.
    • It is goal-directed and adaptive.
    • It transfers to new situations (transfer of training).

    Factors affecting learning

    Learner factors
    • Motivation and interest
    • Maturation and readiness
    • Intelligence and aptitude
    • Health, fatigue, anxiety
    Material factors
    • Meaningfulness
    • Length and difficulty
    • Organisation
    Method factors
    • Distributed (spaced) practice beats massed practice (cramming)
    • Whole vs part method
    • Feedback (knowledge of results)
    • Active recitation
    Environment
    • Noise, light, comfort
    • Teacher and peer support
    RememberFactors = L-M-M-E: Learner, Material, Method, Environment.
    Ivan Pavlov (1849–1936)Russian physiologist. Won the 1904 Nobel Prize for work on digestion; discovered conditioning while studying salivation in dogs.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Classical conditioning

    Learning by association: a neutral stimulus, paired repeatedly with a stimulus that naturally causes a response, comes to cause that response by itself.

    RememberU = Unlearned (natural). C = Conditioned (learned). The bell goes NS → CS; salivation goes UCR → CR.

    Phenomena

    Acquisition

    The CS–CR link is learned through repeated pairing. Best when CS comes about half a second before the UCS (forward / delayed conditioning).

    Extinction

    CS presented repeatedly without UCS → CR weakens and disappears.

    Spontaneous recovery

    After a rest, the extinguished CR suddenly reappears (weaker). So extinction is not forgetting.

    Stimulus generalisation

    Similar stimuli also produce the CR (a different bell tone).

    Discrimination

    Learning to respond only to the CS, not similar stimuli.

    Higher-order conditioning

    A CS is used to condition a new neutral stimulus (light → bell → salivation).

    RememberA-E-S-G-D-H: "All Exams Seem Great During Holidays."

    Related issues and applications

    Key study · Watson & Rayner, 1920

    Little Albert

    An 11-month-old boy was conditioned to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. His fear generalised to other furry things (rabbit, fur coat). It shows phobias can be learned; it is also ethically unacceptable today.

    Taste aversion (Garcia)

    Rats learned to avoid a taste after a single pairing with sickness, even hours later. Biology prepares us to learn some links easily (preparedness).

    Applications

    Treating phobias (systematic desensitisation), advertising, emotional reactions to places and music.

    B. F. Skinner (1904–1990)American behaviourist. Invented the "Skinner box" to study how consequences shape behaviour.Photo: Silly rabbit, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Operant (instrumental) conditioning

    Learning from consequences: behaviour followed by reinforcement is repeated; behaviour followed by punishment decreases.

    E. L. Thorndike · puzzle box (1898)Hungry cats learned by trial and error to escape a box to reach food; escape time fell gradually. Law of effect: responses followed by satisfaction are "stamped in".Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Reinforcement and punishment

    Add something
    (positive +)
    Remove something
    (negative −)
    Behaviour
    INCREASES
    Positive reinforcementAdd a pleasant thing. Praise for homework.
    Negative reinforcementRemove an unpleasant thing. Seat-belt buzzer stops when you buckle up.
    Behaviour
    DECREASES
    Positive punishmentAdd an unpleasant thing. Scolding for coming late.
    Negative punishmentRemove a pleasant thing. No phone for a week.

    Common exam trap: negative reinforcement is not punishment. Reinforcement always increases behaviour.

    Schedules of reinforcement

    ScheduleReinforce after…ExampleResponse pattern
    Continuousevery responseVending machineFast learning, fast extinction
    Fixed ratio (FR)a fixed number of responsesPaid per 10 items madeHigh rate, pause after reward
    Variable ratio (VR)an unpredictable numberLottery, slot machineHighest, steady rate; most resistant to extinction
    Fixed interval (FI)first response after a fixed timeMonthly salary; exam every 4 weeks"Scallop": slow, then a burst near the time
    Variable interval (VI)first response after a varying timeChecking messages; surprise testsSlow, steady rate
    RememberRatio = number of responses, Interval = time. Variable ratio = gambling = hardest to stop.

    Phenomena and related issues

    Shaping

    Reinforcing successive approximations to the target behaviour.

    Chaining

    Linking simple responses into a complex sequence.

    Extinction, generalisation, discrimination

    As in classical conditioning, but for operant responses. A discriminative stimulus signals when reinforcement is available.

    Learned helplessness (Seligman)

    After uncontrollable punishment, animals and people stop trying, even when escape is possible. Linked to depression.

    Biological constraints

    Instinctive drift (the Brelands): trained animals slip back into instinctive behaviour.

    Applications

    Behaviour modification, token economies, classroom management, programmed learning.

    Classical vs operant

    PointClassicalOperant
    LearnsStimulus–stimulus linkResponse–consequence link
    BehaviourInvoluntary (reflex)Voluntary
    TimingStimulus comes before responseConsequence comes after response
    LearnerPassiveActive
    Key namesPavlov, WatsonThorndike, Skinner
    Albert Bandura (1925–2021)Social learning theory. Showed that we learn by watching others, without being reinforced ourselves.Photo: CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Observational learning (modelling)

    Learning by watching others (models) and the consequences of their behaviour.

    RememberA-R-R-M: "All Rivers Reach the Main sea."

    Procedure and phenomena: the Bobo doll studies (1961, 1965)

    Key study · Bandura, Ross & Ross

    Bobo doll

    Children watched an adult hit, kick and shout at an inflatable doll. Later, left alone with toys, they copied the aggression, even the exact words. In the 1965 study, children who saw the model punished imitated less, but when offered a reward they could all reproduce the acts. So learning happened even when it wasn't shown.

    Vicarious reinforcement

    Seeing a model rewarded makes us more likely to imitate.

    Vicarious punishment

    Seeing a model punished makes us less likely to imitate.

    Learning vs performance

    We may learn a behaviour but perform it only when it pays.

    Related issues: media violence and aggression, role models, learning skills by demonstration. Also related: latent learning (Tolman's rats learned a maze without reward and showed it once food was added), showing learning can be cognitive.

    Verbal learning

    Learning of verbal material: words, syllables, lists. It was studied first by Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885), who invented nonsense syllables (CVC: e.g. ZOF, KEB) so meaning wouldn't affect learning.

    Methods

    Serial learning

    Learn items in a fixed order (like a poem).

    Paired-associate learning

    Learn pairs (stimulus–response), like word–meaning in a new language.

    Free recall

    Recall items in any order.

    Serial position effect

    Factors: meaningfulness, familiarity, list length, practice method (spaced is better), and interference from other lists.

    Discrimination learning

    Learning to respond differently to different stimuli: to one stimulus (S+, reinforced) but not another (S−, not reinforced). It is the opposite of generalisation.

    Procedure

    Present two stimuli (e.g. a large and a small circle). Reward responses to one only. With practice, the animal or person responds mainly to S+.

    Lashley's jumping stand: rats learned to jump to the correct card to reach food.

    Phenomena
    • Transposition (Köhler): chickens trained to peck the darker of two greys later chose the even darker new grey, so they learned a relation, not an absolute stimulus
    • Learning sets (Harlow): monkeys "learned how to learn" new discriminations faster

    Everyday examples: telling a ripe from an unripe mango; a child telling "b" from "d"; responding to a red but not a green traffic light.

    Unit II self-test

    Define learning.

    A relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience or practice.

    In Pavlov's study, what is the bell after conditioning?

    The conditioned stimulus (CS).

    What is spontaneous recovery?

    Reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest.

    Negative reinforcement?

    Removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase a behaviour.

    Which schedule is most resistant to extinction?

    Variable ratio.

    Bandura's four processes?

    Attention, retention, reproduction, motivation.

    Who invented nonsense syllables?

    Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885).

    What is transposition?

    Responding to a relationship between stimuli rather than an absolute stimulus (Köhler).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain classical conditioning with its phenomena. 10 marks
    1. Meaning of learning; Pavlov.
    2. Procedure (draw three stages).
    3. Phenomena: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination, higher-order.
    4. Little Albert, taste aversion; applications.
    Describe operant conditioning and schedules of reinforcement. 10 marks
    1. Thorndike's law of effect; Skinner box.
    2. Reinforcement and punishment (2×2).
    3. Schedules (table).
    4. Shaping, chaining, learned helplessness; classical vs operant.
    Write notes on observational, verbal and discrimination learning. 10 marks
    1. Bandura's four processes; Bobo doll; vicarious reinforcement.
    2. Verbal learning: Ebbinghaus, methods, serial position curve.
    3. Discrimination learning: procedure, transposition, learning sets.
    Foundations of Psychology · Unit III

    Memory and Forgetting

    What is memory?

    Memory is the ability to retain and retrieve information over time. It works like a computer: information is put in, kept, and taken out.

    RememberE-S-R: like saving a file: Enter it, Save it, Reopen it.

    Ways to measure retention

    Recall

    Reproduce information without cues (essay question).

    Recognition

    Identify the correct item from options (MCQ). Easier than recall.

    Relearning (savings)

    Time saved when learning something a second time (Ebbinghaus).

    Atkinson–Shiffrin model (1968)

    The multi-store or modal model: information passes through three separate stores.

    The stages in detail

    StoreCapacityDurationEncodingKey study
    Sensory: iconic (visual), echoic (auditory)LargeIconic ≈ 0.25–0.5 s; echoic ≈ 2–4 sRaw sensorySperling (1960): partial-report method
    Short-term (STM)7 ± 2 items (Miller, 1956); more with chunking≈ 18–30 s without rehearsalMainly acousticPeterson & Peterson (1959)
    Long-term (LTM)Practically unlimitedMinutes to a lifetimeMainly semantic (meaning)Bahrick (1975): classmates' names recalled after decades

    Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974)

    Baddeley and Hitch argued STM is not one simple store but an active "mental workspace" with several parts.

    Evidence: we can do a visual and a verbal task together, but not two verbal tasks, because they compete for the same component.

    Types of long-term memory

    Endel Tulving (1972) distinguished episodic from semantic memory.

    RememberEpisodic = Events · Semantic = School facts · Procedural = Practical skills.
    Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850–1909)Über das Gedächtnis (On Memory, 1885). First scientific study of memory, using himself as the only participant and nonsense syllables.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Forgetting

    Forgetting is the inability to retrieve information that was once stored. It may be temporary (tip-of-the-tongue) or permanent.

    Ebbinghaus forgetting curve (1885)

    Causes of forgetting

    1 · Decay (trace decay) theory

    Memory traces fade with time if not used. Fits sensory memory and STM best.

    2 · Interference theory

    Other learning gets in the way. Proactive: old learning blocks new (old phone number blocks the new one). Retroactive: new learning blocks old (a new language makes you forget words of an old one).

    Jenkins & Dallenbach (1924): people remembered more after sleeping than after staying awake, because there was less interference.

    3 · Retrieval failure (cue-dependent)

    The memory is stored but the right cue is missing. Tip-of-the-tongue state. Context- and state-dependent memory.

    4 · Motivated forgetting

    We push painful memories out of awareness (Freud's repression).

    5 · Encoding failure

    Information never got into LTM (e.g. details of a coin you see daily).

    6 · Consolidation failure and brain damage

    Injury disrupts storage. Retrograde amnesia: loss of old memories; anterograde amnesia: can't form new ones (patient H.M.).

    RememberPro = forward, Retro = backward. PROactive: Past Ruins Ongoing. RETROactive: REcent Takes over Remembered Old.

    Improving memory

    • Spaced practice instead of cramming
    • Elaborative rehearsal: link new facts to what you know (deep processing, Craik & Lockhart, 1972)
    • Mnemonics: acronyms, method of loci, peg-word
    • Testing yourself (retrieval practice), like the self-tests here
    • Sleep after studying, and reduce interference

    Unit III self-test

    Three processes of memory?

    Encoding, storage, retrieval.

    Capacity of STM (Miller)?

    7 ± 2 items.

    Duration of iconic memory?

    About a quarter to half a second.

    Four parts of working memory?

    Central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer.

    Episodic vs semantic memory?

    Episodic = personal events; semantic = general facts.

    Proactive interference?

    Old learning interferes with recalling new learning.

    What does the forgetting curve show?

    Most forgetting happens soon after learning, then it slows.

    Who proposed the multi-store model?

    Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the Atkinson–Shiffrin model of memory. 10 marks
    1. Meaning and processes of memory.
    2. Model (draw).
    3. Sensory, STM, LTM: capacity, duration, encoding (table) with studies.
    4. Working memory as a criticism; types of LTM.
    Discuss the causes of forgetting. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; Ebbinghaus forgetting curve (draw).
    2. Decay, interference, retrieval failure, motivated forgetting, encoding failure, amnesia.
    3. Ways to improve memory.
    Foundations of Psychology · Unit IV

    Motivation

    What is motivation?

    From the Latin movere, "to move". Motivation is the process that starts, directs and sustains goal-directed behaviour.

    Activation

    Starting the behaviour.

    Direction

    Choosing a goal.

    Persistence and intensity

    Continuing, and how much effort.

    Types

    Biological (primary) vs social (secondary)

    Biological: inborn, for survival (hunger, thirst). Social: learned from society (achievement, power).

    Intrinsic vs extrinsic

    Intrinsic: doing it because it is enjoyable in itself. Extrinsic: doing it for rewards or to avoid punishment.

    Key concepts

    Instinct

    Inborn, unlearned, fixed patterns found in all members of a species. William McDougall listed many human instincts. Criticised as naming behaviour, not explaining it.

    Need

    A lack or deficit of something (water, food, love).

    Drive

    The tension or arousal a need creates, which pushes us to act. Hull's drive-reduction theory: we act to reduce drives and restore homeostasis (balance).

    Arousal

    Level of alertness. Arousal theory: we seek an optimal level, not zero; explains curiosity and thrill-seeking.

    Incentive

    An external goal that pulls us (money, grades, praise). Drives push; incentives pull.

    RememberNeed = lack (inside) → Drive = push (inside) → Incentive = pull (outside).

    The motivational cycle

    Arousal and performance: Yerkes–Dodson law (1908)

    Biological motives

    Hunger
    • Hypothalamus: lateral hypothalamus (LH) = "start eating"; ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) = "stop eating" (lesion studies on rats)
    • Signals: low blood glucose, stomach contractions (Cannon & Washburn), hormones ghrelin (hunger) and leptin (fullness)
    • Also learned and cultural: smell, time of day, food habits, stress eating
    Thirst
    • Osmotic thirst: salt concentration in cells rises (after salty food)
    • Hypovolemic thirst: fluid volume drops (bleeding, sweating, diarrhoea)
    • Controlled by the hypothalamus; dry mouth is only a minor cue
    Sleep
    • Regulated by the circadian rhythm (about 24 h; suprachiasmatic nucleus, melatonin)
    • Stages: NREM 1–3 (deep sleep in stage 3) and REM (dreaming); a cycle lasts about 90 minutes
    • Functions: restoration, memory consolidation, energy saving
    • Deprivation: poor attention, mood, immunity
    Sex
    • Hormones: testosterone, oestrogen; controlled by hypothalamus and pituitary
    • Unlike hunger, it is not needed for individual survival, only for the species
    • Strongly shaped by learning, culture and values
    • Masters & Johnson's sexual response cycle: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution
    RememberLateral = Let's eat. Ventromedial = Very full.
    David McClelland (1917–1998)Measured the need for achievement (n-Ach) with stories told about TAT pictures. Also studied affiliation and power motives.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Social (learned) motives

    Achievement (n-Ach)

    Desire to excel and meet standards of excellence. High achievers prefer moderate risks, take personal responsibility, want feedback, and persist.

    Developed by parents who encourage independence early.

    Affiliation (n-Aff)

    Need to be with others and form friendly relationships. Increases under fear and stress (Schachter, 1959: anxious people preferred to wait together).

    Approval

    Need for acceptance and praise from others. High need for approval → conformity, people-pleasing.

    Power (n-Pow)

    Need to influence and control others; seek status and prestige. Can be personal (selfish) or socialised (for the group).

    RememberA-A-A-P: "All Ambitious Achievers Plan." (Achievement, Affiliation, Approval, Power)
    Abraham Maslow (1908–1970)Humanistic psychologist. A Theory of Human Motivation (1943); Motivation and Personality (1954).Photo: William Carter, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Maslow's need hierarchy

    Needs are arranged in a pyramid. Lower needs must be reasonably satisfied before higher ones become important.

    LevelNeedExamples
    1PhysiologicalFood, water, sleep, air, warmth
    2Safety and securityShelter, health, job security, freedom from fear
    3Love and belongingnessFriendship, family, intimacy, group membership
    4EsteemSelf-respect, achievement, recognition by others
    5Self-actualisationRealising one's full potential: "What a man can be, he must be."
    RememberBottom to top: P-S-L-E-S: "Please Stop Laughing, Everyone's Studying."

    Key points and evaluation

    D-needs vs B-needs

    Levels 1–4 are deficiency needs: we feel them when they are missing. Self-actualisation is a growth (being) need: it grows stronger as it is met.

    Self-actualisers: realistic, accepting, spontaneous, problem-centred, have peak experiences. Maslow thought fewer than 1% reach this level.

    Evaluation
    • + Simple, intuitive; widely used in education, management, nursing
    • + Positive view of human nature
    • − Order is not fixed: a starving artist may still create
    • − Based on a small, selective sample; hard to test
    • − Western, individualistic: collectivist cultures may rank belonging higher

    Unit IV self-test

    Latin root of motivation?

    Movere: to move.

    Need vs drive vs incentive?

    Need = deficit; drive = internal tension that pushes; incentive = external goal that pulls.

    What is homeostasis?

    The body's tendency to maintain a balanced internal state.

    Yerkes–Dodson law?

    Performance is best at a moderate level of arousal (inverted U).

    Which brain area controls hunger?

    The hypothalamus (LH starts, VMH stops eating).

    Two types of thirst?

    Osmotic and hypovolemic.

    What kind of risks do high n-Ach people prefer?

    Moderate risks.

    Top of Maslow's pyramid?

    Self-actualisation.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the concept of motivation and the motivational cycle. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; components; types.
    2. Instinct, need, drive, arousal, incentive.
    3. Motivational cycle (draw); Yerkes–Dodson (draw).
    Describe biological and social motives. 10 marks
    1. Hunger, thirst, sleep, sex with mechanisms.
    2. Achievement, affiliation, approval, power; McClelland.
    Critically evaluate Maslow's need hierarchy theory. 10 marks
    1. Introduction; pyramid (draw).
    2. Five levels with examples; D vs B needs; self-actualisers.
    3. Strengths and criticisms.
    Foundations of Psychology · Unit V

    Emotion

    What is emotion?

    From the Latin emovere, "to stir up". An emotion is a complex state of feeling that involves three components.

    Physiological

    Body changes: heart rate, breathing, sweating, hormones.

    Cognitive (subjective)

    The inner feeling and how we interpret the situation.

    Behavioural (expressive)

    Facial expression, voice, posture, actions.

    RememberEmotion has a Body, a Brain and a Behaviour side.

    Characteristics of emotions

    Universal: found in all cultures and even infants

    Aroused by a stimulus: a person, event or thought

    Short-lived; a lasting low-level feeling is a mood

    Vary in intensity: annoyance → anger → rage

    Positive or negative (valence)

    Motivate action: fear makes us flee

    Types and classification

    Primary (basic) vs secondary (complex)

    Primary emotions are inborn and universal. Secondary emotions are blends or are learned, like guilt, shame, pride, jealousy.

    Positive vs negative

    Positive: joy, love, pride. Negative: fear, anger, sadness, disgust.

    Plutchik's wheel (1980)

    8 primary emotions in opposite pairs: joy–sadness, trust–disgust, fear–anger, surprise–anticipation. Mixing gives complex ones (joy + trust = love).

    Dimensional view

    Emotions vary on valence (pleasant–unpleasant) and arousal (calm–excited).

    Paul Ekman (b. 1934)American psychologist. Showed that facial expressions of basic emotions are recognised across cultures.Photo: Paul Ekman Group, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Ekman's six primary emotions

    Happiness

    Smile with raised cheeks; "crow's feet" around eyes (Duchenne smile).

    Sadness

    Inner eyebrows raised, lip corners down.

    Anger

    Brows lowered and drawn together, lips pressed.

    Fear

    Eyes wide, brows raised and pulled together, mouth stretched.

    Surprise

    Brows raised high, eyes wide, jaw drops.

    Disgust

    Nose wrinkled, upper lip raised.

    Ekman later added contempt (one-sided lip raise). He also developed the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) and studied micro-expressions.

    Key study · Ekman & Friesen, 1971

    The Fore of Papua New Guinea

    An isolated group with little contact with outsiders matched facial expressions to emotional stories much as Westerners did. This supports the universality of basic emotions. Cultures differ in display rules: when it is acceptable to show an emotion.

    Remember"Happy Sad Angry Friends Surprise Dad." (Happiness, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Surprise, Disgust)

    Physiological correlates of emotion

    Autonomic nervous system (ANS)

    Body changeSympathetic ("fight or flight")Parasympathetic ("rest and digest")
    Heart rateIncreasesDecreases
    BreathingFasterSlower
    PupilsDilateConstrict
    DigestionSlowsResumes
    Sweat glandsMore sweating (GSR rises)Normal
    Adrenal glandsRelease adrenaline, noradrenalineCalm down
    Blood sugarReleased for energyStored

    Brain structures

    Amygdala

    Fear and threat detection; emotional memory. Damage reduces fear.

    Hypothalamus

    Controls the ANS and endocrine responses.

    Limbic system

    Emotion circuit (Papez circuit): amygdala, hippocampus, cingulate cortex.

    Prefrontal cortex

    Regulates and controls emotions; links emotion with decisions.

    Thalamus

    Relays sensory information to the cortex and amygdala.

    Measuring emotional arousal: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and galvanic skin response (GSR). The polygraph ("lie detector") records these, but it measures arousal, not lying, so it can give false results.

    Theories of emotion

    The classic example: you see a snake. What comes first, the racing heart or the fear?

    William James (1842–1910)"We feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." Carl Lange proposed the same idea independently in Denmark.Photo: Notman Studios, public domain, Wikimedia Commons
    1 · James–Lange theory

    Body changes come first; emotion is our perception of them.

    Criticism (Cannon): the same arousal occurs in different emotions; body changes are too slow; animals with the viscera cut off from the brain still show emotion.

    2 · Cannon–Bard theory

    The thalamus sends signals at the same time to the cortex (feeling) and to the body (arousal). Emotion and arousal happen together and independently.

    Criticism: the hypothalamus and limbic system, not the thalamus alone, are central; body feedback does affect emotion.

    3 · Schachter–Singer two-factor theory

    Emotion = physiological arousal + cognitive label. Arousal is general; how we interpret the situation decides which emotion we feel.

    Study (1962): participants injected with adrenaline (epinephrine) who were not told its effects felt either euphoric or angry, depending on how a stooge in the room behaved. Those told what to expect were less affected.

    4 · Lazarus's cognitive-mediational theory

    Our appraisal of the situation comes first and causes both the emotion and the arousal. Primary appraisal: is this relevant or a threat? Secondary appraisal: can I cope?

    Two students fail the same test: one appraises it as a disaster (despair), the other as a challenge (determination).

    RememberJames: Body → Feeling. Cannon: Body + Feeling together. Schachter: Body + Label. Lazarus: Thought → Body + Feeling.

    Comparison

    TheoryOrder of eventsRole of thinking
    James–LangeStimulus → arousal → emotionNone
    Cannon–BardStimulus → (arousal + emotion together)None
    Schachter–SingerStimulus → arousal → label → emotionLabelling the arousal
    LazarusStimulus → appraisal → (emotion + arousal)Central, comes first

    Unit V self-test

    Three components of emotion?

    Physiological, cognitive (subjective), behavioural (expressive).

    Ekman's six primary emotions?

    Happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust.

    Which ANS branch is "fight or flight"?

    Sympathetic.

    Which brain structure is key for fear?

    The amygdala.

    James–Lange in one line?

    We feel afraid because we tremble: arousal comes first, emotion follows.

    Which theory gives the thalamus a central role?

    Cannon–Bard.

    Two factors in Schachter–Singer?

    Physiological arousal and a cognitive label.

    Primary vs secondary appraisal?

    Primary: is this a threat or relevant? Secondary: can I cope with it?

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the meaning, characteristics and classification of emotions. 10 marks
    1. Definition; three components.
    2. Characteristics.
    3. Classification: primary/secondary, positive/negative, Plutchik, Ekman's six with the Fore study.
    Discuss the physiological correlates of emotion. 10 marks
    1. ANS: sympathetic vs parasympathetic (table).
    2. Brain structures.
    3. Hormones; polygraph and its limits.
    Critically compare theories of emotion. 10 marks
    1. Snake example.
    2. James–Lange, Cannon–Bard, Schachter–Singer, Lazarus (draw flows).
    3. Criticisms and comparison table.
    Research Methodology · Unit I

    Research, Variables, Problems and Hypotheses

    What is scientific research?

    Research is a systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation of questions about relationships among phenomena (adapted from F. N. Kerlinger).

    Systematic

    Follows planned steps in order.

    Empirical

    Based on observed data, not opinion.

    Controlled

    Rules out other explanations.

    Objective

    Free from the researcher's personal bias.

    Replicable

    Others can repeat it and check.

    Critical and self-correcting

    Results are open to testing and revision.

    RememberS-E-C-O-R-C: "Science Explains Causes Only by Repeated Checking."

    Steps in research

    1Problem

    Identify and define the research problem.

    2Literature

    Review what is already known.

    3Hypothesis

    State a testable prediction.

    4Design

    Choose method, sample, tools.

    5Data

    Collect and analyse data.

    6Conclusion

    Interpret, report and suggest further research.

    Variables

    A variable is any characteristic that can take different values (vary) across people or conditions: age, anxiety, reaction time, gender.

    RememberIV = what I change. DV = what Depends on it (the result I measure).

    Types of variables

    Independent (IV)

    Manipulated or selected by the researcher; the presumed cause.

    Dependent (DV)

    Measured; the presumed effect.

    Extraneous

    Any other variable that may affect the DV.

    Confounding

    An extraneous variable that changes along with the IV, so we can't tell which caused the effect.

    Intervening (mediating)

    An unseen process between IV and DV (e.g. motivation, fatigue).

    Moderator

    Changes the strength or direction of the IV–DV link (e.g. gender, age).

    Organismic (subject) variable

    A characteristic of the person that can't be manipulated (age, sex, IQ).

    Continuous vs discrete

    Continuous: any value (height). Discrete: categories or whole numbers (number of children).

    Quantitative vs qualitative

    Numbers (scores) vs categories (religion, colour).

    Measurement of dependent variables

    Frequency

    How often (number of errors)

    Latency

    Time to respond (reaction time)

    Duration

    How long (time spent studying)

    Intensity / amplitude

    Strength of response (loudness, GSR)

    Accuracy

    Correct responses

    Scales of measurement (S. S. Stevens)

    ScaleWhat it tellsExampleTrue zero?
    NominalNames or categories onlyGender, roll number, religionNo
    OrdinalOrder or rankClass rank, Likert agree–disagreeNo
    IntervalOrder + equal intervalsTemperature in °C, IQ scoreNo
    RatioEqual intervals + true zeroReaction time, weight, number correctYes
    RememberNOIR (French for "black"): Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio.

    Control of independent and extraneous variables

    Controlling the IV

    Manipulate it precisely: define the levels clearly, present them the same way to everyone (standardised instructions), and check the manipulation worked.

    Techniques for extraneous variables
    • Elimination: remove it (soundproof room)
    • Constancy: keep it the same for all (same time of day)
    • Matching: equate groups on it (same IQ)
    • Randomisation: random assignment spreads it evenly
    • Counterbalancing: vary order (AB / BA) to cancel order effects
    • Balancing: equal numbers in each group
    • Blind / double-blind: control expectancy and experimenter bias
    • Statistical control: e.g. ANCOVA
    Remember"Every Careful Mind Randomises, Counterbalances and Blinds."

    Research problem

    A research problem is a question about the relationship between two or more variables that can be answered by collecting data. Kerlinger: a good problem asks about a relation, is stated clearly as a question, and can be tested empirically.

    Example

    "Does daily meditation reduce exam anxiety among postgraduate students?"

    Types of research problems

    Descriptive

    What is happening? "How common is screen addiction among teens?"

    Relational

    Are variables related? "Is self-esteem related to academic performance?"

    Causal

    Does one cause another? "Does feedback improve learning?"

    Problems can also be classed as theoretical (testing a theory) vs practical (solving a real problem), and as new vs replication.

    Sources of research problems

    Personal experience

    Observations in daily life, clinics, classrooms.

    Theory

    Deducing predictions from theories.

    Literature review

    Gaps, contradictions and "future research" sections of papers.

    Practical and social issues

    Policy needs, social problems (suicide, addiction).

    Replication

    Repeating studies in new settings, e.g. in India.

    Experts and discussions

    Teachers, seminars, conferences.

    Criteria for a good problem

    • Researchable and specific
    • Novel and significant
    • Feasible: time, money, skills, access
    • Ethically acceptable
    • Interesting to the researcher

    Hypothesis

    A hypothesis is a tentative, testable statement about the expected relationship between two or more variables. It is an educated guess to be tested.

    Example

    "Students who meditate daily will report lower exam anxiety than students who do not."

    Characteristics of a good hypothesis

    Testable: can be checked with data

    Clear and precise: no vague terms

    States a relationship between variables

    Consistent with known facts and theory

    Simple (parsimonious)

    Specific about variables and population

    Falsifiable: could be shown to be wrong

    Types of hypotheses

    TypeMeaningExample
    Null (H0)No difference or relationship"There is no difference in anxiety between meditators and non-meditators."
    Alternative (H1)There is a difference or relationship"There is a difference in anxiety…"
    Directional (one-tailed)States the direction"Meditators will have lower anxiety."
    Non-directional (two-tailed)Difference, direction not stated"Meditators and non-meditators will differ in anxiety."
    Research (working)The researcher's actual prediction, in wordsUsually directional
    StatisticalIn symbols for testingH0: μ1 = μ2

    We never "prove" a hypothesis: we either reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis, usually at the .05 or .01 level of significance.

    Functions of a hypothesis

    • Gives direction to research: what to study and measure
    • Tells which data to collect and which design and statistics to use
    • Links theory to observation; tests and extends theory
    • Provides a framework for drawing conclusions
    • Prevents blind, aimless research

    Unit I self-test

    IV vs DV?

    IV is manipulated (the cause); DV is measured (the effect).

    What is a confounding variable?

    An extraneous variable that varies with the IV, so its effect can't be separated from the IV's.

    Four scales of measurement?

    Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio (NOIR).

    What does counterbalancing control?

    Order effects in within-subjects designs.

    Three types of research problems?

    Descriptive, relational, causal.

    Null hypothesis?

    A statement of no difference or no relationship.

    Directional vs non-directional?

    Directional states which group will be higher; non-directional only says they differ.

    Long-answer outlines

    What is a variable? Explain types and control of variables. 10 marks
    1. Definition; IV–DV diagram.
    2. Types (table).
    3. Measuring DVs; NOIR scales.
    4. Control techniques.
    Define hypothesis. Explain its characteristics, types and functions. 10 marks
    1. Definition with example.
    2. Characteristics.
    3. Types (table).
    4. Functions; relation to research problem.
    Research Methodology · Unit II

    Types of Research

    The big picture

    Research types differ in how much control the researcher has, and so in whether they can show cause and effect.

    TypeIV manipulated?Random assignment?Shows cause?
    Descriptive / surveyNoNoNo
    CorrelationalNoNoNo
    Ex post factoNo (already occurred)NoNo (weak inference)
    Quasi-experimentalYesNoPartly
    ExperimentalYesYesYes

    Descriptive research

    Describes the characteristics of a person, group or situation as it is. It answers "what", not "why".

    Case study

    In-depth study of one person or unit (Freud's cases; patient H.M.).

    Naturalistic observation

    Watching behaviour in its natural setting without interfering (Jane Goodall's chimpanzees).

    Archival research

    Using existing records (census, hospital files).

    Survey research

    Collects information from a sample using questionnaires or interviews, to describe attitudes, beliefs or behaviour in a population.

    Cross-sectional survey

    Different groups at one point in time (e.g. stress in 18-, 30- and 50-year-olds this year).

    Longitudinal survey

    The same group followed over time (panel study). Shows change but is slow and costly, with drop-outs.

    Pros: large samples, quick, cheap, generalisable if sampled well. Cons: self-report bias, social desirability, no causal conclusions, wording effects.

    Correlational research

    Measures two or more variables to see whether and how strongly they are related. The result is a correlation coefficient (r) from −1 to +1.

    RememberCorrelation ≠ causation. Ice-cream sales and drowning rise together, but heat causes both (a third variable).

    Use when variables can't be manipulated (ethics or practicality), for prediction, and as a first step before experiments. Problems: third-variable problem and directionality problem (does X cause Y or Y cause X?).

    Ex post facto research

    Latin for "after the fact". The IV has already occurred naturally; the researcher looks back to find its link with the DV. The IV can't be manipulated.

    Examples

    Effect of parental divorce on children's adjustment; smoking and lung cancer; effect of an earthquake on PTSD.

    Strengths

    • Only ethical way to study harmful causes
    • Real-life variables
    • Generates hypotheses

    Limitations

    • No control or random assignment
    • Self-selection: groups may differ in many ways
    • Causal conclusions are weak

    Experimental research

    The researcher manipulates the IV, randomly assigns participants to conditions, controls extraneous variables, and measures the DV. It is the only method that shows cause and effect.

    Experimental group

    Receives the treatment (IV).

    Control group

    Doesn't receive it (or gets a placebo); used for comparison.

    Random assignment

    Every participant has an equal chance to be in any group, so groups start equal.

    Internal validity

    Confidence that the IV, not something else, caused the change in the DV.

    External validity

    How well results generalise to other people, places and times.

    Lab experiments have high internal validity but can be artificial (low ecological validity).

    Quasi-experimental research

    Like an experiment, but without random assignment, usually because groups already exist (classrooms, hospitals).

    Non-equivalent groups design

    Compare an existing treatment group with an existing comparison group, with pre-test and post-test.

    Interrupted time-series design

    Measure the DV many times before and after an intervention (e.g. accident rates before and after a helmet law).

    Useful in real settings, but groups may differ at the start (selection bias), so causal claims are weaker.

    Field study vs field experiment vs lab experiment

    PointLab experimentField experimentField study
    SettingArtificial labReal lifeReal life
    IV manipulated?YesYesNo (observed)
    ControlHighModerateLow
    RealismLowHighVery high
    ExampleAsch's line studyPiliavin's subway helping study (1969)Studying classroom climate in a school

    Qualitative research

    Studies meanings and experiences in depth, using words rather than numbers. Small samples, open-ended data, and the researcher is part of the process.

    Methods

    In-depth interviews, focus groups, participant observation, case studies, diaries.

    Approaches
