    Phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, narrative, thematic analysis.

    Example

    "How do first-generation college students experience their first semester?"

    PointQuantitativeQualitative
    DataNumbersWords, images
    AimTest hypotheses, measureExplore, understand meaning
    SampleLarge, randomSmall, purposive
    AnalysisStatisticsThemes, coding
    ApproachDeductive, objectiveInductive, interpretive

    Mixed-method research

    Combines quantitative and qualitative methods in one study to get both breadth and depth (triangulation).

    Convergent (parallel)

    Collect both at the same time and compare.

    Explanatory sequential

    Quantitative first, then qualitative to explain the results.

    Exploratory sequential

    Qualitative first, then build a quantitative tool or test.

    Unit II self-test

    Which research type can show cause and effect?

    Experimental research (manipulation + random assignment + control).

    Cross-sectional vs longitudinal?

    Different groups at one time vs the same group over time.

    Range of a correlation coefficient?

    From −1 to +1.

    What does "ex post facto" mean?

    "After the fact": the IV has already occurred.

    Main difference between quasi and true experiments?

    Quasi-experiments lack random assignment.

    Field study vs field experiment?

    Both in real settings, but only the field experiment manipulates the IV.

    What is triangulation?

    Using multiple methods or data sources to check findings.

    Long-answer outlines

    Compare experimental, quasi-experimental and ex post facto research. 10 marks
    1. Control spectrum (draw).
    2. Each type: meaning, example, pros and cons.
    3. Comparison table.
    Write notes on survey and correlational research. 10 marks
    1. Survey: types, pros/cons.
    2. Correlational: r, scatter plots (draw), correlation ≠ causation.
    Research Methodology · Unit III

    Sampling

    What is sampling?

    Sampling is the process of selecting a small group (sample) from a larger group (population) so we can study the sample and draw conclusions about the population.

    Population

    The whole group we want to know about (all PG psychology students in India).

    Sampling frame

    The actual list from which the sample is drawn (enrolment lists).

    Representative sample

    A sample whose characteristics match the population's.

    Purpose of sampling

    • Saves time, money and effort
    • Studying the whole population is often impossible
    • Allows more careful data collection on fewer people
    • Allows generalisation from sample to population

    Determining sample size

    Larger sample needed when…
    • The population is very varied (heterogeneous)
    • We expect a small effect
    • We need high precision and confidence
    • We will compare many subgroups
    • Many people may drop out
    Ways to decide
    • Power analysis (e.g. using G*Power): sample needed to detect an effect
    • Formula for estimating a proportion: n = Z²·p·q / e². With 95% confidence (Z = 1.96), p = 0.5 and 5% error: n ≈ 384
    • Rules of thumb: at least 30 per group for experiments

    Types of sampling

    Probability sampling

    MethodHowExample
    Simple randomEvery member has an equal chance; lottery or random-number tableDraw 100 names from a list of 2,000 students
    SystematicChoose every kth person after a random start (k = N / n)Every 20th name on the roll
    StratifiedDivide into strata (subgroups), then sample randomly from each, often in proportionSample men and women in their population ratio
    ClusterRandomly select whole groups (clusters), then study everyone in themRandomly pick 10 colleges and test all students there
    MultistageSample in stages: states → districts → schools → studentsNational surveys

    Non-probability sampling

    MethodHowExample
    Convenience (accidental)Whoever is easy to reachYour own classmates
    Purposive (judgemental)Researcher chooses people with specific characteristicsOnly parents of autistic children
    QuotaFill set quotas for subgroups, chosen non-randomly50 men and 50 women from a market
    SnowballParticipants refer others; for hidden groupsDrug users, migrant workers
    RememberProbability: "Some Students Sit in Class Mornings" (Simple, Systematic, Stratified, Cluster, Multistage). Non-probability: "Cats Prefer Quiet Snow" (Convenience, Purposive, Quota, Snowball).

    Factors influencing sampling decisions

    Size

    Bigger samples are more accurate but costlier. Balance precision against resources.

    Accessibility

    Can you reach the people? Hidden or busy groups may need snowball or purposive sampling.

    Cost

    Money, time and staff limit the method: random national samples are expensive; convenience samples are cheap.

    Also

    Research aim, nature of the population, availability of a sampling frame, type of analysis, ethics.

    Sampling error

    Sampling error is the difference between a sample statistic and the true population value, arising because we study only part of the population.

    Random sampling error

    Due to chance. It gets smaller as sample size increases and can be estimated (standard error).

    Non-sampling error / sampling bias

    Systematic error from a faulty method: wrong sampling frame, non-response, volunteer bias, measurement errors. A bigger sample does not fix bias.

    Classic example · 1936

    The Literary Digest poll

    A huge sample of about 2.4 million predicted the wrong US presidential winner because names came from telephone and car-owner lists, which over-represented wealthier voters. Large but biased samples still mislead.

    Unit III self-test

    Population vs sample?

    Population = whole group of interest; sample = the selected part studied.

    Sample size for ±5% at 95% confidence (p = 0.5)?

    About 384.

    Stratified vs cluster sampling?

    Stratified samples individuals from every subgroup; cluster randomly picks whole groups.

    When to use snowball sampling?

    For hard-to-reach or hidden populations.

    Does a bigger sample remove bias?

    No. It reduces random error, not systematic bias.

    Quota vs stratified?

    Both use subgroups, but quota selection within groups is non-random.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the meaning, purpose and types of sampling. 10 marks
    1. Population, sample, frame (draw).
    2. Purpose.
    3. Probability methods (table).
    4. Non-probability methods (table).
    Discuss sample size, factors influencing sampling and sampling error. 10 marks
    1. Determining sample size; formula.
    2. Size, accessibility, cost and other factors.
    3. Random error vs bias; Literary Digest example.
    Research Methodology · Unit IV

    Research Design

    What is a research design?

    Kerlinger: research design is "the plan, structure and strategy of investigation conceived so as to obtain answers to research questions and to control variance."

    Plan

    The overall scheme: what to do, from hypothesis to analysis.

    Structure

    The outline of how variables are arranged (groups, conditions).

    Strategy

    Methods of data collection and analysis.

    Purpose: control of variance (the MAX-MIN-CON principle)

    MAXimise systematic variance

    Make the IV levels clearly different so its effect shows.

    MINimise error variance

    Reduce random errors: reliable measures, standard conditions.

    CONtrol extraneous variance

    Randomise, match, hold constant, block.

    RememberMAX-MIN-CON: MAXimise the IV's effect, MINimise error, CONtrol the rest.

    Characteristics and criteria of a good design

    Answers the research question adequately

    Controls extraneous variables (internal validity)

    Generalisable (external validity)

    Objective, reliable and replicable

    Economical and feasible: time, money, ethics

    Flexible enough for the problem

    Between-groups designs

    Each participant is in only one condition; conditions are compared across different groups.

    Randomised two-group design

    Participants randomly assigned to an experimental and a control group (post-test only, or pre-test–post-test).

    Randomised multi-group design

    Three or more levels of one IV (0, 1, 2 hours of practice). Analysed with one-way ANOVA.

    + No carry-over or practice effects. − Needs more participants; individual differences between groups add error.

    Within-group (repeated measures) designs

    The same participants take part in all conditions; each person acts as their own control.

    Advantages

    • Fewer participants needed
    • Individual differences controlled, so more sensitive (powerful)

    Problems: order effects

    • Practice (improvement) and fatigue (decline)
    • Carry-over: one condition affects the next
    • Solution: counterbalancing (half do AB, half BA; or ABBA)
    PointBetween-groupsWithin-group
    Participants per conditionDifferent peopleSame people
    Sample neededLargerSmaller
    Individual differencesAdd errorControlled
    Order effectsNoneYes: counterbalance
    StatisticsIndependent t-test, ANOVAPaired (correlated) t-test, repeated-measures ANOVA

    Factorial designs

    Study two or more IVs at the same time. Every level of one IV is combined with every level of the other. A 2 × 2 design has 2 IVs with 2 levels each = 4 conditions.

    Example: memory scoreQuiet roomNoisy room
    MorningCondition 1Condition 2
    NightCondition 3Condition 4
    Main effect

    The effect of one IV on its own, averaged over the other (e.g. noise lowers memory overall).

    Interaction effect

    The effect of one IV depends on the level of the other. Shown by non-parallel lines on a graph.

    + Efficient: tests several IVs and their interaction in one study; more like real life. − Many conditions need many participants; complex interactions are hard to interpret. Analysed with two-way ANOVA.

    Randomised block design

    Participants are first grouped into blocks that are similar on a nuisance variable (e.g. IQ: high, average, low). Then, within each block, they are randomly assigned to treatment conditions.

    Block (IQ)Method AMethod BMethod C
    Highrandomrandomrandom
    Averagerandomrandomrandom
    Lowrandomrandomrandom

    Removes the nuisance variable's effect from error variance, making the design more sensitive. Analysed with two-way ANOVA (treatment × block).

    Matched group design

    Participants are paired on a relevant variable (e.g. pre-test score, age, IQ). One of each pair is then randomly assigned to each condition.

    Advantages

    • Groups start equal on the key variable
    • Reduces error variance
    • No order effects (unlike within-group)

    Disadvantages

    • Matching is time-consuming
    • Can match only on a few variables
    • Losing one participant loses the pair

    Analysed with a correlated (paired) t-test for two groups.

    Single-subject (small-N) designs

    One participant (or a few) is measured repeatedly over time, during baseline (A) and treatment (B) phases. Common in clinical and behaviour-modification work (Skinner's tradition).

    AB design

    Baseline then treatment. Simple but weak: change might be due to something else.

    ABA / ABAB (reversal)

    Withdraw and reintroduce treatment. Strong evidence; ABAB ends on treatment (more ethical).

    Multiple-baseline

    Start treatment at different times across behaviours, people or settings. Used when withdrawal is unethical or impossible.

    + Detailed, useful in therapy, needs few participants. − Hard to generalise; possible carry-over.

    Unit IV self-test

    Kerlinger's definition of research design?

    The plan, structure and strategy of investigation conceived to answer research questions and control variance.

    What is MAX-MIN-CON?

    Maximise systematic variance, minimise error variance, control extraneous variance.

    Main problem of within-group designs?

    Order effects (practice, fatigue, carry-over), controlled by counterbalancing.

    How many conditions in a 2 × 3 design?

    Six.

    How does an interaction look on a graph?

    Non-parallel lines.

    Randomised block vs matched group?

    Block groups many people on a nuisance variable and randomises within blocks; matched pairs individuals.

    Why is ABAB stronger than AB?

    Behaviour changes each time treatment is introduced or removed, ruling out other causes.

    Long-answer outlines

    Define research design. Explain its purpose and criteria. 10 marks
    1. Kerlinger's definition; plan, structure, strategy.
    2. MAX-MIN-CON.
    3. Criteria: validity, control, generalisability, feasibility.
    Compare between-groups, within-group and factorial designs. 10 marks
    1. Between vs within (table).
    2. Factorial: main effects, interaction (draw).
    3. Block and matched designs; single-subject (draw ABAB).
    Research Methodology · Unit V

    Data Collection, Report Writing and Ethics

    Interview

    A face-to-face (or phone/online) conversation in which the researcher asks questions to collect information.

    Structured

    Fixed questions in fixed order. Easy to compare and quantify; less depth.

    Semi-structured

    Guide of key questions with freedom to probe. Most common in psychology.

    Unstructured

    Free conversation around a topic. Rich depth; hard to compare.

    Advantages

    • In-depth information; can clarify and probe
    • Works with illiterate people and children
    • Observes non-verbal cues

    Disadvantages

    • Time-consuming and costly
    • Interviewer bias; social desirability
    • Needs trained interviewers

    Tips: build rapport, use neutral language, avoid leading questions, record accurately with consent.

    Observation

    Systematically watching and recording behaviour as it happens.

    Participant vs non-participant

    Participant: the observer joins the group (covert or overt). Non-participant: watches from outside.

    Naturalistic vs controlled

    Natural setting (playground) vs a lab or set-up situation (one-way mirror).

    Structured vs unstructured

    Structured uses checklists and coding schemes (time sampling, event sampling); unstructured records freely.

    Problems

    Observer bias, reactivity (people behave differently when watched: the Hawthorne effect), ethics of covert observation. Use more than one observer for inter-observer reliability.

    Questionnaire vs schedule

    PointQuestionnaireSchedule
    Who fills it?Respondent fills itResearcher / enumerator fills it while asking
    Respondent must beLiterateCan be illiterate
    DeliveryPost, email, online, in personFace to face
    Cost and coverageCheap, large samplesCostly, smaller samples
    Response rateOften lowHigh
    Clarifying doubtsNot possiblePossible

    Writing good questions

    Question types

    Closed (yes/no, multiple choice): easy to analyse. Open (free answer): richer but harder to code.

    Avoid
    • Leading questions ("Don't you agree…")
    • Double-barrelled questions (two in one)
    • Jargon, ambiguity, double negatives
    • Overly long questionnaires

    Always pilot test the questionnaire on a small group first.

    Rating scales

    Tools for recording a judgement of degree: how much of a trait or attitude a person shows.

    Graphic rating scale

    Mark a point on a line from "very poor" to "excellent".

    Numerical scale

    Rate from 1 to 5 or 1 to 10.

    Likert scale

    Agreement with statements: strongly agree … strongly disagree (5 points).

    Semantic differential (Osgood)

    Bipolar adjective pairs: good ___ ___ ___ bad.

    Checklist

    Tick the traits that apply.

    Common rating errors

    Halo effect

    One good trait colours all ratings.

    Leniency / severity

    Rating everyone too high or too low.

    Central tendency error

    Avoiding extremes; rating everyone "average".

    Logical error

    Assuming traits go together (intelligent, so hard-working).

    RememberRating errors are H-L-C-L: "Happy Lecturers Can't Lie." (Halo, Leniency, Central tendency, Logical)

    Research report in APA style (7th edition)

    The American Psychological Association (APA) format is the standard structure for psychology reports and papers.

    #SectionWhat goes in it
    1Title pageTitle, author, affiliation, course, instructor, date
    2AbstractAbout 150–250 words: aim, method, results, conclusion; keywords
    3IntroductionBackground, literature review, rationale, hypotheses
    4MethodParticipants (sample, sampling), materials/measures (tests with reliability and validity), design, procedure
    5ResultsDescriptive and inferential statistics, tables and figures (no interpretation)
    6DiscussionInterpretation, link to past research, limitations, implications, future research
    7ReferencesAlphabetical, hanging indent
    8AppendicesQuestionnaires, raw data, consent forms
    RememberT-A-I-M-R-D-R-A: "Ten Ants In My Room Dance Really Awkwardly."

    APA citation basics

    In-text citation

    (Festinger & Carlsmith, 1959) or Festinger and Carlsmith (1959) found… Three or more authors: (Bandura et al., 1961).

    Reference list: journal article

    Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203–210.

    Reference list: book

    Kerlinger, F. N. (1973). Foundations of behavioral research (2nd ed.). Holt, Rinehart and Winston.

    Style points

    Past tense for method and results; numbers for statistics (e.g. t(28) = 2.45, p = .02); avoid biased language.

    Ethical issues in psychological research

    Guided by the APA Ethics Code and, in India, institutional ethics committees (and ICMR guidelines for health research). Every study should be approved by an ethics committee / IRB before data collection.

    Informed consent

    Participants agree freely after knowing the purpose, procedure, risks and benefits. For children: parental consent + child's assent.

    Right to withdraw

    Participants can leave at any time without penalty.

    Protection from harm

    No physical or psychological harm beyond everyday risk.

    Confidentiality and privacy

    Data kept secure and anonymous; identities not revealed.

    Deception and debriefing

    Deception only if essential and harmless; participants must be debriefed (told the truth) afterwards.

    Honest reporting

    No fabrication, falsification or plagiarism; credit co-authors; share data.

    RememberC-W-H-C-D: "Can We Help Clients Decently?" (Consent, Withdraw, Harm, Confidentiality, Debriefing)

    Studies that changed the rules

    Milgram, 1963

    Obedience

    Severe stress and deception; the experimenter's "prods" pressured participants to continue, undermining their right to withdraw.

    Zimbardo, 1971

    Stanford prison experiment

    Guards became abusive; stopped after 6 days. The researcher's dual role compromised participant protection.

    Watson & Rayner, 1920

    Little Albert

    Conditioned fear in an infant with no attempt to remove it afterwards.

    Tuskegee, 1932–72

    Syphilis study

    Treatment withheld from Black American men; led to the Belmont Report (1979).

    Unit V self-test

    Three types of interview?

    Structured, semi-structured, unstructured.

    What is the Hawthorne effect?

    People change their behaviour because they know they are being observed.

    Questionnaire vs schedule?

    A questionnaire is filled in by the respondent; a schedule is filled in by the researcher.

    What is the halo effect?

    One positive trait colours ratings of all other traits.

    Order of APA report sections?

    Title page, abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, references, appendices.

    What is debriefing?

    Explaining the true purpose of the study to participants afterwards, especially after deception.

    Long-answer outlines

    2. Observation: types, problems.
    3. Questionnaire vs schedule (table); question writing.
    4. Rating scales and errors.

    1. Hourglass (draw).
    2. Each section with contents.
    3. Citation examples.

    2. Six principles with explanation.
    3. Classic unethical studies.
